title: Pressure engineering of the excitonic moiré-potential landscape and exciton-charge interplay in semiconductor moiré superlattices
authors: Wenbing Li, Tianhao Yue, Wenjian Su, Zhexu Shan, Chen Xu, Jichen Zhou, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Liguo Ma, Yuanfeng Xu, Shiyao Zhu, Yang Gao, Yanhao Tang
abstract: Semiconductor moiré superlattices, owing to strongly bound excitons and pronounced electronic correlation, have emerged as an intriguing solid platform for exploring correlated bosonic phenomena, where the moiré potential landscape plays a central role. Hydrostatic pressure allows continuous, in-situ tuning of this landscape, but remains underexplored because of experimental challenges. Here we integrate a diamond anvil pressure cell with high quality dual gated WSe2/WS2 twisted bilayers and perform cryogenic optical spectroscopy. We observe distinct pressure evolutions of moiré intralayer excitons, which reveal drastic modulation of the excitonic moiré-potential landscape captured by a continuum model and suggest the capability of engineering the exciton-band topology. Moreover, we demonstrate efficient pressure control over the interplay between charges and both intralayer and interlayer excitons: the intralayer charge-transfer exciton becomes less sensitive to doping, likely due to reduced charge-transfer character; in contrast, the interlayer exciton exhibits enhanced exciton-charge repulsion. Our results establish hydrostatic pressure as a powerful tuning knob for engineering bosonic quasiparticles and Bose-Fermi interactions in moiré materials.
summary: This paper reports on using hydrostatic pressure in moiré semiconductor superlattices to actively engineer the excitonic potential landscape. By combining high-pressure spectroscopy with continuum modeling, the authors show that pressure controls exciton binding character and dictates the system's topological state. This establishes pressure as a versatile tool for controlling correlated bosonic quasiparticles.
main_problem: The study investigates how hydrostatic pressure can be used to engineer the excitonic moiré-potential landscape and tune the complex interplay between excitons and free charges in semiconductor moiré superlattices.
main_result: The research demonstrates that pressure acts as a powerful tuning knob, enabling the engineering of the exciton band topology and modifying the nature of exciton-charge interactions, such as suppressing charge-transfer character.
method: The work combines cryogenic optical spectroscopy (PL/RC) performed inside a diamond anvil cell with continuum theoretical modeling to analyze the spectral evolution.
model_or_system: The physical system is semiconductor moiré superlattices, specifically twisted TMD bilayers ($	ext{WSe}_2/	ext{WS}_2$). The theoretical framework uses a continuum model based on the moiré potential to predict changes in exciton band topology and interaction strengths.
key_observables: Moiré intralayer exciton resonances, exciton-charge interaction strengths ($	ext{U}_{e-	ext{X}_{	ext{I}}}$), moiré potential parameters ($V, \Delta$), and the topological invariant (Chern number).
important_parameters:
Hydrostatic pressure (up to 3.6 GPa), doping concentration ($
u$), and the twist angle of the bilayer.
main_assumptions: The continuum model is used to capture potential evolution, and the image-charge model is employed to calculate screening effects, though limitations exist regarding non-uniform doping.
figures_summary: Figures show pressure dependence of exciton resonances (RC/PL), theoretical fits to the moiré potential parameters, and phase diagrams mapping the topological transitions (Chern number) as a function of pressure-induced potential changes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents experimental measurements across varying pressures, correlating the observed spectral shifts and changes in exciton character with predictions from the continuum model, culminating in the demonstration of topological tunability.
why_interesting: The ability to use external stimuli like pressure to tune fundamental many-body parameters (like topological invariants and interaction strengths) in solid-state systems is highly relevant to understanding strongly correlated phases in quantum materials.
